clinicalPearls: The most severe of the glycolytic enzymopathies, combining chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with progressive neuromuscular disease
Inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, frequently with consanguinity, and most patients present in infancy
A progressive neurological syndrome with spasticity, dystonia, tremor and motor neurone-type weakness typically emerges after the first months of life
Recurrent infections and increased susceptibility to bacterial illness are characteristic and contribute to early mortality
Cardiac involvement and sudden death may occur, adding to the poor prognosis
The metabolic hallmark is a marked accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate in red cells, with reduced enzyme activity on assay and a confirmatory TPI1 mutation
Management is supportive with transfusion, folate and vigilant treatment of infections; no disease-modifying therapy exists and splenectomy offers limited benefit
reference.pathophysiology: Triosephosphate isomerase interconverts dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, ensuring both triose phosphates feed into the ATP-yielding steps of glycolysis. Deficiency causes accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate and a fall in glycolytic energy production; in the red cell this shortens survival to produce a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia, while in neural and muscle tissue the same energy failure, together with toxic effects of the accumulated substrate, drives a progressive and often fatal neuromuscular disorder with heightened susceptibility to infection.
additionalDifferentials: Glucose phosphate isomerase deficiency with neuromuscular features
Hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neurone disorders of infancy
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of red-cell dihydroxyacetone phosphate accumulation
Full blood count, reticulocytes and blood film
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Neurological assessment with neurophysiology and imaging
Molecular testing of the TPI1 gene
redFlags: Progressive neuromuscular deterioration with respiratory compromise
Cardiac involvement predisposing to sudden death
Severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection
reference.prognosis: The classic infantile form carries a poor prognosis, with progressive neurological decline, susceptibility to infection and frequent death in early childhood; rare milder variants with residual enzyme activity have a better course.
pitfalls: Focusing on the anaemia while missing the emerging neuromuscular syndrome
Underestimating infection risk and delaying antimicrobial treatment
Expecting splenectomy to substantially alter the systemic disease
Failing to offer genetic counselling given the recessive inheritance and severe phenotype
management: Manage the chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with folic acid supplementation and red-cell transfusion during severe anaemia or aplastic crises
Prevent and treat infection aggressively with vaccination and prompt antibiotics given the marked susceptibility to bacterial illness
Provide neuromuscular supportive care with physiotherapy and management of spasticity and dystonia, adding respiratory support as weakness progresses
Undertake cardiac surveillance for arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy given the risk of sudden death
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across haematology, neurology, cardiology and paediatrics, with early palliative involvement in the severe infantile form
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for the autosomal recessive TPI1 defect
